header: Ghani Ur Rehman etc. Vs. Hazrat Ullah & others.
Mr. Abid Ayub, Advocate for the petitioner.
Mr. Muhammad Taif Khan, Advocate, for the respondent No.1
Mr. Saad Ul Maabood Khattak, Advocate, for the respondent
body: MUHAMMAD NAEEM ANWAR, J: - This single judgment shall also decide Civil Revision Petition No. 1106-P of 2023, titled Fayyaz Ghani v. Hazrat Ullah and others, as both petitions arise out of Suit No. 161/1 of 2018 and involve interconnected questions concerning the ownership, possession and transfer of the disputed property.

2. The petitioner in the instant petition sought his impleadment in the aforementioned suit, claiming to have acquired ownership rights in the disputed property through Mutation No. 12541 dated 19.02.2020, whereby, in exchange, he claims to have acquired property comprised in Khasra Nos. 1687, 1688 and 3261. His application for impleadment was declined by the learned trial Court, and the appeal preferred against the said order was also dismissed. Meanwhile, the learned Civil Judge-II, Peshawar, decreed the suit instituted by respondents No. 1 and 2, whereby they had sought a declaration of their ownership and possession over land measuring 03 Kanals and 12 Marlas, comprised in Khasra Nos. 1303, 1306, 1381, 1687 and 1688, situated in the revenue estate of Sarband. They specifically claimed possession over Khasra Nos. 1687 and 1688 and asserted that defendant No. 1, Fayyaz Khan, had no right, title or interest therein. The suit was contested by defendant No. 1, who is the petitioner in the connected revision petition, on the assertion that he was owner in possession of the disputed property and had raised construction thereon in exercise of his ownership rights. Notwithstanding the controversy raised in the written statement, the learned trial Court decreed the suit through summary judgment. The appeal preferred by defendant No. 1 was also dismissed, giving rise to the connected Civil Revision Petition No. 1106-P of 2023. Thus, both petitions call into question the orders declining impleadment of the present petitioner and the decree passed against defendant No. 1 through summary proceedings, together with the appellate judgments upholding the respective orders.

4. It appears from the record that the predecessor-in-interest of the plaintiffs/respondents acquired rights in the property through Mutation No. 2552, stated to have been attested on 29.12.1954, whereby he purchased land comprised in fifteen survey numbers and was recorded as a Hissadar in Khasra Nos.

3441 and 3448 in the Jummabandi for the year 1955-56. It is pertinent to mention that he (Qudrat Ullah), had purchased land measuring 12 Kanals and 01 Marla out of a total area of 24 Kanals and 15 Marlas, comprised in fifteen survey numbers, through referred to above mutation. The disputed Khasra Nos. 1303, 1306, 1381, 1687 and 1688 form part of the land claimed through the said transaction. On the strength of the aforesaid acquisition, the respondents asserted ownership over land measuring 03 Kanals and 12 Marlas, with a specific claim of possession over Khasra Nos. 1687 and 1688. However, the revenue entries contained in the Jamabandi for the year 2011- 2012 disclose that Shamshad Khan son of Muqarrab Khan was recorded as Ghair Dakhilkar, whereas his status vis-à-vis the recorded owners, as reflected in the column of Lagaan, was described as Bila Lagaan Bawaja-e-Qabza. Of particular significance is the entry relating to Shah Faisal s/o Khan Khel, arrayed as defendant No. 31 in the suit, who was recorded as an owner in the relevant property. The petitioner claims to have acquired his interest through the said Shah Faisal by virtue of Mutation No. 12541. The mutation, particularly its column No. 13, reflects an exchange transaction with reference to Mutation No. 12240, entered on 20.01.2020 and attested on 19.02.2020. The vendor, Shah Faisal, had himself acquired his ownership rights through Mutation Nos. 9710, 9711, 9712, 9713 and 9718. The application for impleadment filed by the petitioner was declined primarily on the ground that his acquisition was hit by Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, embodying the doctrine of lis pendens. The learned Courts below further observed that, in the event of his dispossession, the petitioner could avail himself of the remedy of partition. Such an approach, however, overlooks an important distinction between the effect of a transfer pendente lite and the substantive rights of a transferee who claims through a co-owner. The petitioner, having derived his alleged title through Shah Faisal, stepped into the shoes of his vendor and acquired no better title than that possessed by the latter. Nevertheless, the nature and extent of the rights so acquired, particularly in the context of the petitioner's assertion of possession and construction over the disputed property, could not have been brushed aside without proper adjudication.

5. It is a settled principle of law that possession of one coowner is, in the absence of circumstances establishing exclusion or ouster, deemed to be possession on behalf of all the coowners. A co-sharer cannot ordinarily be dispossessed from joint property merely at the instance of another co-sharer, unless the property has been partitioned by metes and bounds or the claimant otherwise establishes an independent legal entitlement to exclusive possession. The principle was enunciated by the august Supreme Court in Ali Gohar Khan v. Sher Ayaz and others (1989 SCMR 130), wherein it was held that possession of one co-owner is deemed to be possession of all co-owners. Consequently, a decree for possession against a co-sharer cannot, in the ordinary course, be executed through his physical eviction from joint property before its lawful partition. This principle also finds reflection in Order XXI Rule 35 CPC, which provides for delivery of possession in execution of a decree for immovable property. Where the decree concerns joint property and the judgment-debtor is a co-sharer, the executing Court must have regard to the nature of the decree and the respective rights of the co-sharers. A decree for possession cannot, merely by virtue of its execution, be employed to dispossess a co-owner from joint property to which his undivided share extends. The nature and extent of possession deliverable must, therefore, be determined in accordance with the applicable provisions of law and the rights established by the parties.

6. In the present case, the petitioner asserts that his vendor, Shah Faisal, was a recorded co-owner and that, through the exchange transaction, he acquired the vendor's interest in the property along with possession thereof. He further maintains that he raised construction at the site in pursuance of his claimed ownership and possession. Whether the vendor was indeed a coowner in the specific Khasra numbers forming the subject matter of the suit, whether the petitioner acquired the vendor's share therein, and whether possession was actually delivered to him pursuant to the transaction are questions which bear directly upon the rights of the parties. These matters required examination of the relevant revenue record, the nature and extent of the vendor's title, the exchange transaction and the evidence concerning possession and construction.

7. As regards the doctrine of lis pendens, embodied in Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, the legal position is equally well settled. The doctrine operates to preserve the subject matter of litigation during the pendency of proceedings in which rights to immovable property are directly and specifically in question. Its object is to prevent any party to the litigation from transferring or otherwise dealing with the disputed property in a manner that may prejudice the rights of the other party under the eventual decree. A transferee pendente lite is, therefore, bound by the result of the litigation and takes the property subject to the rights ultimately determined therein, even where he was not impleaded as a party to the proceedings or had no actual or constructive notice of the pending litigation. The foundation of this doctrine does not rest upon the question of notice to the transferee; rather, it is founded upon necessity and public policy, so that the administration of justice may not be frustrated by successive transfers of the disputed property during the pendency of litigation. Were such transfers permitted to defeat the rights of the parties, there would be no finality to judicial proceedings and the successful litigant would be deprived of the fruits of the decree. Reference in this regard may be made to Muhammad Ashraf Butt and others v. Muhammad Asif Bhatti and others (PLD 2011 SC 905) and Simla Banking Industrial Co. Ltd. v. Firm Luddar Mal (AIR 1959 Punj 490). It is, however, equally important to appreciate that the doctrine of lis pendens does not, by itself, render a transfer pendente lite void or non-existent. Its legal effect is that the transfer remains subservient to the rights of the parties as determined in the pending litigation, and the transferee cannot claim a position superior to that of his transferor. Thus, if the transferor's rights are defeated or restricted by the eventual decree, the transferee is equally bound by that determination. Conversely, where the transferor possessed an independent subsisting interest in the property, the nature and extent of such interest and its legal consequences must be determined in accordance with law. In the present matter, the petitioner's acquisition during the pendency of the suit undoubtedly attracted consideration of Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882. However, the mere fact that the transaction was affected pendente lite could not, without further examination, furnish a conclusive answer to the questions whether the vendor was a co-owner, what interest he possessed in the disputed Khasra numbers, whether that interest was transferred to the petitioner through the exchange transaction, and what legal effect the transaction would have upon the petitioner's claim of possession. The doctrine of lis pendens binds the transferee to the outcome of the pending litigation; it does not authorize the Court to presume facts that have yet to be established or to dispense with adjudication of material questions arising from the pleadings.

8. The above controversy assumes particular significance in the context of the manner in which the suit was decided. Order XV-A CPC provides a specific mechanism for disposal of a claim or defence through summary judgment, without subjecting the parties to a regular trial. However, such power is not unqualified and cannot be exercised merely because the Court considers the controversy capable of summary determination. The provision expressly requires the Court to be satisfied that the opposing party has no real prospect of succeeding in the claim or defence and that there is no genuine dispute as to any material fact requiring trial, with the result that the applicant is entitled to judgment as a matter of law. Summary judgment may also be granted where the parties agree to such determination and the Court considers it appropriate. The jurisdiction under Order XV-A CPC is, therefore, confined to cases in which the material facts are either undisputed or sufficiently established through the documentary material on record, and no genuine issue of material fact remains which requires determination through the regular process of trial. It is not intended to curtail the right of a party to have a genuine factual controversy adjudicated through evidence, nor can it be employed as a substitute for a regular trial where the determination of the parties' rights requires examination of witnesses, scrutiny of disputed documents or resolution of conflicting factual assertions. The Court, while considering an application for summary judgment, is also required to construe the documentary evidence in a manner most favourable to the respondent, and any doubt regarding the existence of a genuine issue of material fact must be resolved against the applicant. Thus, summary judgment is appropriate only where the controversy falls squarely within the parameters prescribed by Order XV-A CPC, the opposing party has no real prospect of succeeding, and no material factual dispute survives for adjudication. It may be resorted to where the dispute is essentially legal or where the material facts are not genuinely controverted and the determination does not require a deeper factual inquiry. It cannot, however, be granted where the rights of the parties depend upon resolution of disputed questions of ownership, possession, the nature of a transaction or other material circumstances requiring evidence and proper appreciation thereof. Tested on the aforesaid touchstone, the present controversy was not amenable to summary adjudication. The petitioner's acquisition through Shah Faisal, the latter's status as a co-owner, the precise extent of his share in the disputed Khasra numbers, the nature and legal effect of the exchange transaction, and the petitioner's assertion that possession was delivered to him and that he had raised construction over the property were all material questions requiring determination. These were not incidental or inconsequential matters; rather, they went to the root of the competing claims of ownership and possession. The written statement raised a substantive defence which could not have been rejected without examining the evidence necessary to establish or negate the same.

9. The learned trial Court, therefore, could not have decreed the suit through summary judgment without first determining whether the controversy satisfied the statutory requirements of Order XV-A CPC. Equally, the learned appellate Court failed to appreciate that the dispute involved genuine questions of fact which could not be conclusively resolved merely by invoking the doctrine of lis pendens. The observation that the petitioner, even if dispossessed, could avail himself of the remedy of partition was also legally unsustainable in the absence of a determination as to whether his vendor was a co-owner in the disputed property and whether the petitioner had lawfully acquired the vendor's interest. A person claiming through a co-owner cannot be relegated to the remedy of partition without first examining the very basis of his claim and the nature of the rights acquired by him. The question whether the petitioner is entitled to retain possession as a transferee of a co-sharer, or whether his claim is subject to the rights established by the respondents in the pending litigation, could only be answered after proper adjudication of the relevant facts and law.

10. In view of the foregoing discussion, it is evident that both the learned Courts below failed to appreciate the material legal and factual aspects of the controversy. In particular, the decree passed through summary judgment was not sustainable, as the matter involved genuine disputes of material fact requiring adjudication through a regular trial. The learned Courts below, by overlooking these aspects and proceeding to determine the competing claims without recording the requisite evidence, committed material legal errors warranting interference by this Court. Consequently, both petitions are accepted. The judgments and orders passed by the learned Courts below, including the order declining the petitioner's application for impleadment and the judgment and decree passed in favour of respondents No. 1 and 2 through summary proceedings, together with the respective appellate judgments, are hereby set aside. The application of petitioner for his impleadment as defendant is allowed. The matter is remitted to the learned trial Court for decision afresh, the plaintiff shall submit amended plaint by impleading the petitioner as defendant. Learned trial court shall decide the suit afresh, after affording the parties an opportunity to lead evidence and determining their respective rights in accordance with law. The learned trial Court shall specifically examine the applicability and legal effect of the doctrine of lis pendens under Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882; the ownership status and extent of the share of Shah Faisal in the disputed Khasra numbers; the nature and legal effect of the exchange transaction in favour of the petitioner; and the petitioner's assertion of possession and construction over the property. The question whether the petitioner acquired the rights of a co-owner and, if so, the extent and legal incidents of such rights shall also be determined on the basis of the evidence brought on record. The matter shall not be prejudiced by any observation made herein on the merits of the competing claims, which shall be determined independently in accordance with law. The parties are directed to appear before the learned Civil Judge-II, Peshawar, on 26.11.2026. There shall be no order as to costs.
J UD G E Abdul Wahid, JSS
(SB) Hon’ble Mr. Justice Muhammad Naeem Anwar.
